title: Battles in the Supreme Court -- Ch. 11: Epilogue: THE REAL VICTORY
keywords: I study, I reflect, I pray and stick to my conscience
rule and majesty of the law
primary_topics: Chapter 11 of 'Battles in the Supreme Court' -- the Epilogue, in which CJP explains that the real victory of a jurist lies not in conforming to conventional wisdom but in the free and untrammeled expression of his deepest convictions
His account of how he decides and writes -- 'I study, I reflect, I pray and stick to my conscience' -- offered to a colleague wavering over whether to change his vote on a Motion for Reconsideration

His defense of a divided Court: unanimity on volatile issues is not to be expected of a free and thinking Court, and the people's rights are best safeguarded by magistrates who expound from varying viewpoints
A valedictory survey of the colleagues retiring around him and of the younger successors in whose probity, balance and fearlessness he finds consolation and hope
sub_topics: The opening scene: a fellow justice privately asks how CJP makes up his mind and writes his opinions, and he answers in one sentence about study, reflection, prayer and conscience

His elaboration to that colleague: fifty years hence their opinions will still be dissected by lawyers, law students and the public, and beyond that they must answer to the Lord and Supreme Judge by the very standards with which they judged others

His own development on the bench: an early struggle to conform to precedent and conventional judicial wisdom, giving way to the fulfillment of expressing himself openly even when alone in the minority
His tribute to the justices who likewise deliberated actively and wrote voraciously, and his hope that their tribe increase

The roll of departures -- Justices Feliciano and Padilla already retired, and Justice Regalado, Chief Justice Narvasa and Justice Romero reaching compulsory retirement on October 13, 1998, November 30, 1998 and August 1, 1999
His recognition of the short-tenured justices Hermosisima, Torres, Francisco and Martinez, whose brief stints were not their fault and who still enriched jurisprudence
The thesis of the epilogue: the mission of a jurist and of the Court does not depend on the number of unanimous decisions, and the Court should be a marketplace of free ideas

His portrait of the courage the work requires -- pursuing lonely causes against majoritarian precedent, presidential displeasure and public ridicule, with no interest in litigants but only in principles, causes and philosophies
His closing personal note: over eight years more in the Court ahead of him, three already immensely enjoyed, and a hope of participating proactively in future battles of consciences

stances.claim: A magistrate's duty is to study, reflect, pray and follow his conscience, knowing that his opinions will be dissected for decades and that he must ultimately answer for how he judged others.
stances.rhetorical_move: personal testimony turned into counsel, with an appeal to posterity and to divine accounting

stances.claim: Jurists are never diminished by their dissents, only by their reckless and thoughtless concurrences; being in the minority, or even alone, is more fulfilling than conforming to conventional judicial wisdom.
stances.rhetorical_move: epigrammatic inversion, backed by his own account of growing out of an early deference to precedent

stances.claim: A divided Court better serves the tripartite system and the people's rights than a uniform and hackneyed voice, because the Court should be a veritable marketplace of free ideas.
stances.rhetorical_move: institutional defense of disagreement, recasting division as a feature rather than a defect

stances.claim: The real victory of jurists lies in the free and untrammeled expression of their scruples and credos, unaffected by the fortunes or misfortunes of individual litigants.
stances.rhetorical_move: redefinition of victory as the book's closing thesis, stated as a principle rather than an outcome

notable_anecdotes: In the heat of deliberations a fellow justice, torn between upholding his earlier vote and changing it on reconsideration, privately asked CJP how he made up his mind -- and got the reply 'I study, I reflect, I pray and stick to my conscience.'

CJP pressed the question further, asking his colleague how he wanted to be remembered by his grandchildren and great-grandchildren, and how he would answer at the pearly gates if judged by the standards with which he judged others.

He confesses that in the early months of his incumbency he struggled to conform to precedent and conventional judicial wisdom, and only later found more fulfillment in speaking openly even when alone.
He closes the book on a personal count: over eight years still ahead of him in the Court, and three already 'immensely enjoyed.'

Citizens judging the Court by its independence rather than its unanimity

one_paragraph_summary: The Epilogue to 'Battles in the Supreme Court' opens with a private exchange during deliberations: a fellow justice, torn between upholding his earlier vote and changing it on a Motion for Reconsideration, asked Justice Panganiban how he made up his mind and wrote his opinions, and received the reply, 'I study, I reflect, I pray and stick to my conscience.' Pressing further, CJP reminded his colleague that fifty years hence their decisions would still be discussed and dissected by lawyers, law students and the public, and that beyond that audience they would have to account for their actions at the pearly gates before a Lord and Supreme Judge who might apply the very standards by which they had judged others. He confesses that during the early months of his incumbency he struggled to conform to precedent and conventional judicial wisdom, but learned over the years that he found greater fulfillment in expressing himself openly and decisively even when in the minority or alone, repeating his conviction that jurists are never diminished by their dissents, only by their reckless and thoughtless concurrences. He salutes the colleagues who likewise deliberated actively and wrote voraciously, wishes that their tribe increase, and surveys the departures around him -- Feliciano and Padilla already gone, Regalado, Narvasa and Romero reaching compulsory retirement, and the short-tenured Hermosisima, Torres, Francisco and Martinez who nonetheless left their imprints -- while finding consolation in the probity and fearlessness of their younger successors. His closing thesis is institutional: the mission of a jurist and of the Court does not depend on the number of unanimous decisions, for a free and thinking Court cannot be expected to speak with a uniform and hackneyed voice; the people's rights are best served by a divided Court that is a veritable marketplace of free ideas. The real victory of jurists, he concludes, lies not in conforming to conventional wisdom but in the courage to express their deepest thoughts and to pursue lonely causes, caring nothing for the fortunes of individual litigants and everything for principles, causes and philosophies. He ends personally, with over eight years still ahead of him and three already immensely enjoyed.
